A Roadmap for Content Validity Used in Scale Development Studies *  
DOI number: 10.17556/erziefd.297741  
Selami YEŞİLYURT **, Cüneyt ÇAPRAZ ***  
Date received: 13.03.2017 Date accepted: 26.01.2018  
The aim of this study is to present a roadmap to researchers on how to conduct content validity studies by introducing content validity ratios and the content validity index. The roadmap is provided through an example study, taking into account the technique developed by Lawshe (1975) and the criteria specified by Ayre and Scally (2014). Twenty-six experts participated in the sample study. The "Expert Form," which evaluates 66 items, was used as the data collection tool. Keywords: Content validity ratio, content validity index, content validity criterion, scale development, expert opinions. *The aim of this study is to provide researchers with a roadmap for conducting content validity studies by introducing content validity ratios and the content validity index. ** Atatürk University, Faculty of Education, Department of Biology Education, Erzurum, Turkey; selamiy@atauni.edu.tr *** Alaaddin Keykubat University Faculty of Education, Department of Primary School Teaching, Alanya, Turkey; cuneyt.capraz@alanya.edu.tr  
Selami YEŞİLYURT, Cüneyt ÇAPRAZ  
It is of great importance to accurately identify attitudes and opinions in education and psychology (Özbek, Kahya & Özgen, 2007; Yurdugül, 2005). This highlights the significance of scale development studies. However, the primary issue to be considered in scale development is the validity of the measurement tool (Brains, Willnat, Manheim & Rich, 2011). Because validity is a crucial criterion for the credibility and generalizability of a scientific study (Basham & Sedlacek, 2009; Yıldırım & Şimşek, 2013). In validity studies, special attention should be paid to the consistency of the relationship between the scale to be developed and the characteristic intended to be measured. Through this type of study, known as content validity, the extent to which each item serves the purpose is revealed. In this way, a developed scale will contain items with strong representational power for the subject under study, rather than unrelated statements irrelevant to the topic (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Basham & Sedlacek, 2009; Brinkman, 2009; Frank-Stromberg & Olsen, 2004; Wilson, Pan, & Schumsky, 2012). In content validity studies, also called logical or rational validity studies (Shuttleworth, 2016), a preliminary study must be conducted in which sufficient expert opinions are obtained to determine the coverage power of the scale item for the feature intended to be measured (Allen & Yen, 2002; Basham & Sedlacek, 2009; Brinkman, 2009; Büyüköztürk, 2005; Ercan & Kan, 2004; Lawshe, 1975; McMillan & Schumacher, 2010; Otrar & Argın, 2015; Rubio et al., 2003). Because, in such preliminary studies, if the number of experts is sufficiently large (between 5-40), the validity of the scale to be prepared will also be high (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). With content validity, after determining whether the scale items are a sample of the universe in which the researchers are interested, appropriate items within the scope can be written to form a scale (Cronbach & Meehl, 1951; Rubio et al., 2003). However, content validity studies based on expert opinions are qualitative studies (Shuttleworth, 2016). Therefore, the data obtained should be converted into quantitative data by calculating the content validity ratios (CVR) and content validity index (CVI) (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Büyüköztürk, 2005; Demiralp & Kazu, 2012; McGartland et al., 2003). After this process, referred to as content analysis, a usable scale with sufficient coverage can be prepared that has advantages such as increasing construct validity related to the construct the scale aims to measure, conducting preliminary item analyses, and controlling the number of item factors (Büyüköztürk, 2005; Demiralp & Kazu, 2012). Various techniques have been developed to determine content validity (Cohen, 1960; Davis, 1992; Lawshe, 1975; Lindell & Brandt, 1999; Lindell, Brandt, & Whitney, 1999; James, Demaree, & Wolf, 1993; Tinsley & Weiss, 1975). The most commonly used is the technique developed by Lawshe (1975) (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). This technique stands out for its simplicity and ease of use compared to alternatives (Wilson et al., 2012). However, as will be discussed in detail in the methods section, Wilson and colleagues (2012) and Ayre and Scally (2014) noted deficiencies regarding the content validity criterion of this technique and revised the “Lawshe technique” accordingly. As a result, in developed scales, it is important to determine, based on expert opinions, whether the items in the scale are sufficient in covering and gathering the factual and/or judgmental data needed. The aim of this study is to present a roadmap for how content validity studies can be conducted by introducing content validity ratios and the content validity index through an exemplary study. A Path for Content Validity Used in Scale Development Studies…

The example study for which content analysis was conducted is a qualitative study through which theoretical processes and theoretical form were obtained. However, the qualitative data obtained were converted into quantitative data in order to test the consistency between expert opinions and to facilitate the analysis. Considering studies conducted on determining content validity (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Cohen, 1960; Davis, 1992; James, Demaree, & Wolf, 1993; Lawshe, 1975; Lindell & Brandt, 1999; Lindell, Brandt, & Whitney, 1999; Tinsley & Weiss, 1975; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012), the technique developed by Lawshe (1975) stands out for its simplicity and usability (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). This was taken into account in the study. In their review on content validity, Veneziano and Hooper (1997) demonstrated, along with their reasons, that the technique introduced by Lawshe (1975) provides objective and definitive results. Subsequently, Wilson et al. (2012) and Ayre & Scally (2014) confirmed this situation through their studies. However, Wilson et al. (2012) and Ayre & Scally (2014) criticized the critical CVR values published by Lawshe (1975) regarding content validity criteria, and later recalculated and revised these values. In this study, taking these criticisms into account, a roadmap for the recalculated content validity computations—which can be referred to as the "modified Lawshe technique"—is presented below with an example study. In the study, the following stages were basically followed:
1. Formation of the expert group. 2. Preparation of the draft scale form and collection of expert opinions. 3. Data analysis. a. Calculation of content validity ratios (CVR=Content Validity Ratio). b. Calculation of content validity index (CVI=Content Validity Index). 4. Deciding whether each item should be included in the scale based on the content validity ratio and content validity index criteria (This section is presented in the findings section.). 2.1. Formation of the Expert Group  
The quality and number of experts (between 5 and 40) play a significant role in obtaining objective results in the calculations to determine content validity (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). This consideration was taken into account in the present study. The experts participating in the study were selected from among faculty members (26 individuals) working at the Faculty of Education, Department of Biology Education, Atatürk University, using a convenience sampling method to facilitate access. 2.2. Preparation of the Draft Scale Form and Collection of Expert Opinions  
In the Lawshe (1975) technique, expert opinions for each item are rated using three categories: “the item measures the intended construct,” “the item is related to the construct but is unnecessary,” and “the item does not measure the intended construct.” However, in this study, the rating categories for expert opinions found in Lawshe’s (1975) technique were reorganized as “Appropriate,” “Appropriate but Needs Revision,” and “Should be Removed.” Similar rating categorizations are present in the literature (Alisinanoğlu & Şimşek, 2013; Ateş Çobanoğlu, 2013). In the sample study, the expert form to be used as the data collection tool consisted of a total of 69 items. Of these, 66 items were aimed at determining content validity, while the remaining 3 collected demographic characteristics of the experts. The experts were asked to select one of the above rating categories for each of the 66 items on the form. In calculating the content validity ratios for the scale, “Appropriate” was scored as 3, “Appropriate but Needs Revision” as 2, and “Should be Removed” as 1. Additionally, beyond the standard rating in the Lawshe (1975) technique, the researchers requested that for every item an expert marked as needing revision, they answer the question “If your answer is that the item should be revised, what is your suggestion for improvement?”; and for every item marked for removal, “If your answer is that the item should be removed, why?” Thus, experts were asked to provide their opinions in writing for each item as needed. 2.3. Data Analysis
In the study, in order to determine the content validity of the items to be included in the scale, the qualitative data obtained based on expert opinions were converted into quantitative data by calculating CVR and CVI. In this conversion process, CVR was calculated first, followed by CVI. The calculations were performed using Microsoft Excel 2013 (Figure 1). 2.3.a. Calculation of Content Validity Ratio (CVR)

Here, Nu represents the number of experts who rated the item as “Appropriate,” and N indicates the total number of experts who provided their opinion on the item. The CVR value ranges between -1 (absolute rejection) and +1 (absolute acceptance). If all participants rate any item in the scale as “Appropriate,” the CVR value for that item becomes 1. However, considering the possibility of error or chance, this value is accepted as 0.99. In this case, if more than half of the participants rate any item on the scale as “Appropriate,” the Content Validity Ratio (CVR) will take a value between 0 and 0.99. According to the CVR equation: if half of the experts give an “Appropriate” rating to an item, CVR=0; if more than half provide an “Appropriate” rating, CVR>0; and if less than half provide an “Appropriate” rating, CVR<0. If the CVR is zero (0) or negative (less than zero), the item is considered to lack content validity. Therefore, such items are directly eliminated from the scale (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Wilson et al., 2012). According to Lawshe (1975), for each item with a positive value, the content validity criterion (CVRcritical) at the significance level α=0.05 should be checked. CVRcritical is the minimum required CVR value to ensure that the rate of “Appropriate” ratings for each item is not due to chance, and it is therefore used to determine whether an item is truly appropriate for inclusion. CVR values are used to determine the minimum number of experts who must approve an item in order to decide whether it is necessary or unnecessary. However, the CVR value varies depending on the number of experts. Lowell Schipper calculated these critical values according to certain criteria, and Lawshe (1975), utilizing Schipper’s calculations, prepared a table of Minimum/Critical CVR values. However, in his study, Lawshe did not provide information on how the values in this table were calculated (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). Later, Wilson et al. (2012) identified a calculation error in the table published by Lawshe (1975) and recalculated these critical CVR values (CVRcritical) using different methods. Ayre and Scally (2014) reviewed both the critical CVR value studies conducted by Wilson et al. (2012) and those by Lawshe (1975). In this evaluation, based on the critical value calculations made by Wilson et al. (2012), they argued that it is not possible to decide whether items are necessary or unnecessary using these critical values and that these critical values are not reliable. On the other hand, they noted that the critical values shown in Lawshe’s (1975) article are reliable for making decisions about items, but they are not sufficient. Unlike Lawshe, Ayre and Scally (2014) emphasized that even if the number of experts participating in the study increases or decreases by just one, the critical CVR values would change. They prepared a new table of minimum/critical CVR values (CVRcritical) for different numbers of experts at α=0.05 significance level, using various statistical analyses (Table 2). As a result, considering the arguments put forth in the studies on CVRcritical by Lawshe (1975), Wilson et al. (2012), and Ayre & Scally (2014), it was decided that the CVRcritical values established by Ayre & Scally (2014) would be used as the basis in the sample study. In light of this basis, Table 2 shows that, at a significance level of α=0.05, the CVRcritical value for 26 experts is 0.385. 2.3.b. Calculation of Content Validity Index (CVI)
The Content Validity Ratio (CVR) is a statistical tool used for the acceptance or rejection of specific items. Once items are defined to be included in the scale through the determination of CVR, the CVI is then calculated for the entire test. In this case, the mean of the CVR values of the items deemed appropriate for inclusion on the scale is calculated to obtain the CVI value. It is important to note that the content validity index should not be confused with the correlation coefficient. The CVI represents the degree of overlap observed between the functional capacity of a defined job performance domain and the performance observed in the test under investigation. Functionally, the CVI is the average percentage of overlap between the test items and the job performance domain (Lawshe, 1975). Selami YEŞİLYURT, Cüneyt ÇAPRAZ
Yurdugül (2005) stated that it is important to determine in how many dimensions the characteristic to be measured is gathered, and emphasized that if the characteristic is collected in more than one dimension, a CVI should be obtained for each dimension. Taking this emphasis into account, under the assumption that the sample scale used in the study has only one dimension, the CVI value was calculated as 0.691 for that single dimension (Table 3). Based on the opinions provided by a total of 26 experts on the items, CVR values were obtained with reference to the formula given in “Equation 1,” and items with a CVR of 0 (zero) or negative (below zero)—specifically Item 1 and Item 2—were directly removed from the scale (Table 3). Subsequently, it was determined whether the CVR values of items with values greater than zero were statistically significant and thus whether these items would remain in the scale, by referring to the CVRcritical values presented in Table 2. According to Table 2, the CVRcritical value for 26 experts who participated in the study is 0.385. Accordingly, when Table 3 is examined, it is observed that after removing two items (Items 1 and 2) from the scale, the CVR values of 6 of the remaining 64 items (Items 4, 16, 27, 28, 29, and 30) are lower than the critical CVR value (CVRcritical = 0.385). Therefore, these 6 items, which fall below this critical value, were also removed from the draft scale being developed. As a result, 58 items remained in the sample scale. The CVI value for the sample study was calculated after removing 8 items from the scale and was determined to be 0.691. The fact that the obtained CVI value is greater than the CVRcritical value (CVI>CVRcritical) indicates that the content validity of the remaining items on the scale is statistically significant (Ateş Çobanoğlu, 2013; Batdı, 2013; Lawshe, 1975; Öngöz, 2011). In other words, when the CVI and CVRcritical values are compared, if the CVI value is less than the CVRcritical value, it is stated that the remaining items in the scale do not possess content validity (Lawshe, 1975). Accordingly, since the values obtained in the sample study indicate that the CVI (0.691) > CVRcritical (0.385), the content validity of the remaining items in the scale (58 items) is statistically significant. After the content validity analyses of the sample study, the remaining 58 items for which at least one expert indicated a “needs revision” opinion were reviewed again and revised in line with expert feedback, and ultimately, a scale possessing content validity was obtained. 4. Discussion and Conclusion
In this sample study, the content validity ratio and content validity index were introduced, and a roadmap was provided for conducting content analysis in scale development studies in a simple and practical way. In scale development studies, the reliability of the measurement tool is related to its stability. In this case, validity studies that consider what is intended to be measured with the measurement tool and whether the items measure accurately for their intended purpose come to the forefront. The validity of measurement obtained from assessment tools will vary depending on the intended purpose of the measurement (Ercan & Kan, 2004; Kalaycı, 2016; Leech, Barrett, & Morgan, 2005). Content validity studies, which reveal the extent to which the scale and each item on the scale serve their intended purpose, are processes that convert qualitative studies based on expert opinions into statistical quantitative studies (Ercan & Kan, 2004; Shuttleworth, 2016; Yurdugül, 2005). Through this process, referred to as content analysis in scale development studies, the quality of the scale and its items is enhanced and procedural and temporal efficiency is achieved (Büyüköztürk, 2005; Demiralp & Kazu, 2012; Yurdugül, 2005). The qualifications of the experts are also highly important for ensuring consistent and unbiased results (Shuttleworth, 2016; Yurdugül, 2005). Consequently, by following the roadmap presented in this study, a useful scale with adequate content validity can be developed—one that offers advantages such as increasing construct validity for the targeted construct, conducting preliminary item analyses, and controlling the number of item factors. DOI number: 10.17556/erziefd.297741  
Selami YEŞİLYURT **, Cüneyt ÇAPRAZ ***  
Date received: 13.03.2017 Date accepted: 26.01.2018  
The aim of this study is to present a roadmap to researchers on how to conduct content validity studies by introducing content validity ratios and the content validity index. The roadmap is provided through an example study, taking into account the technique developed by Lawshe (1975) and the criteria specified by Ayre and Scally (2014). Twenty-six experts participated in the sample study. The "Expert Form," which evaluates 66 items, was used as the data collection tool.

discourses.source_txt: Because validity is a crucial criterion for the credibility and generalizability of a scientific study (Basham & Sedlacek, 2009; Yıldırım & Şimşek, 2013). In validity studies, special attention should be paid to the consistency of the relationship between the scale to be developed and the characteristic intended to be measured. Through this type of study, known as content validity, the extent to which each item serves the purpose is revealed. In this way, a developed scale will contain items with strong representational power for the subject under study, rather than unrelated statements irrelevant to the topic (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Basham & Sedlacek, 2009; Brinkman, 2009; Frank-Stromberg & Olsen, 2004; Wilson, Pan, & Schumsky, 2012). In content validity studies, also called logical or rational validity studies (Shuttleworth, 2016), a preliminary study must be conducted in which sufficient expert opinions are obtained to determine the coverage power of the scale item for the feature intended to be measured (Allen & Yen, 2002; Basham & Sedlacek, 2009; Brinkman, 2009; Büyüköztürk, 2005; Ercan & Kan, 2004; Lawshe, 1975; McMillan & Schumacher, 2010; Otrar & Argın, 2015; Rubio et al., 2003). Because, in such preliminary studies, if the number of experts is sufficiently large (between 5-40), the validity of the scale to be prepared will also be high (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). With content validity, after determining whether the scale items are a sample of the universe in which the researchers are interested, appropriate items within the scope can be written to form a scale (Cronbach & Meehl, 1951; Rubio et al., 2003). However, content validity studies based on expert opinions are qualitative studies (Shuttleworth, 2016). Therefore, the data obtained should be converted into quantitative data by calculating the content validity ratios (CVR) and content validity index (CVI) (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Büyüköztürk, 2005; Demiralp & Kazu, 2012; McGartland et al., 2003). After this process, referred to as content analysis, a usable scale with sufficient coverage can be prepared that has advantages such as increasing construct validity related to the construct the scale aims to measure, conducting preliminary item analyses, and controlling the number of item factors (Büyüköztürk, 2005; Demiralp & Kazu, 2012). Various techniques have been developed to determine content validity (Cohen, 1960; Davis, 1992; Lawshe, 1975; Lindell & Brandt, 1999; Lindell, Brandt, & Whitney, 1999; James, Demaree, & Wolf, 1993; Tinsley & Weiss, 1975). The most commonly used is the technique developed by Lawshe (1975) (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). This technique stands out for its simplicity and ease of use compared to alternatives (Wilson et al., 2012). However, as will be discussed in detail in the methods section, Wilson and colleagues (2012) and Ayre and Scally (2014) noted deficiencies regarding the content validity criterion of this technique and revised the “Lawshe technique” accordingly. As a result, in developed scales, it is important to determine, based on expert opinions, whether the items in the scale are sufficient in covering and gathering the factual and/or judgmental data needed. The aim of this study is to present a roadmap for how content validity studies can be conducted by introducing content validity ratios and the content validity index through an exemplary study.

discourses.source_txt:
Preparation of the Draft Scale Form and Collection of Expert Opinions  
In the Lawshe (1975) technique, expert opinions for each item are rated using three categories: “the item measures the intended construct,” “the item is related to the construct but is unnecessary,” and “the item does not measure the intended construct.” However, in this study, the rating categories for expert opinions found in Lawshe’s (1975) technique were reorganized as “Appropriate,” “Appropriate but Needs Revision,” and “Should be Removed.” Similar rating categorizations are present in the literature (Alisinanoğlu & Şimşek, 2013; Ateş Çobanoğlu, 2013). In the sample study, the expert form to be used as the data collection tool consisted of a total of 69 items. Of these, 66 items were aimed at determining content validity, while the remaining 3 collected demographic characteristics of the experts. The experts were asked to select one of the above rating categories for each of the 66 items on the form. In calculating the content validity ratios for the scale, “Appropriate” was scored as 3, “Appropriate but Needs Revision” as 2, and “Should be Removed” as 1. Additionally, beyond the standard rating in the Lawshe (1975) technique, the researchers requested that for every item an expert marked as needing revision, they answer the question “If your answer is that the item should be revised, what is your suggestion for improvement?”; and for every item marked for removal, “If your answer is that the item should be removed, why?” Thus, experts were asked to provide their opinions in writing for each item as needed.

According to the CVR equation: if half of the experts give an “Appropriate” rating to an item, CVR=0; if more than half provide an “Appropriate” rating, CVR>0; and if less than half provide an “Appropriate” rating, CVR<0. If the CVR is zero (0) or negative (less than zero), the item is considered to lack content validity. Therefore, such items are directly eliminated from the scale (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Wilson et al., 2012). According to Lawshe (1975), for each item with a positive value, the content validity criterion (CVRcritical) at the significance level α=0.05 should be checked. CVRcritical is the minimum required CVR value to ensure that the rate of “Appropriate” ratings for each item is not due to chance, and it is therefore used to determine whether an item is truly appropriate for inclusion.

However, in his study, Lawshe did not provide information on how the values in this table were calculated (Ayre & Scally, 2014; Lawshe, 1975; Veneziano & Hooper, 1997; Wilson et al., 2012). Later, Wilson et al. (2012) identified a calculation error in the table published by Lawshe (1975) and recalculated these critical CVR values (CVRcritical) using different methods. On the other hand, they noted that the critical values shown in Lawshe’s (1975) article are reliable for making decisions about items, but they are not sufficient. Unlike Lawshe, Ayre and Scally (2014) emphasized that even if the number of experts participating in the study increases or decreases by just one, the critical CVR values would change. They prepared a new table of minimum/critical CVR values (CVRcritical) for different numbers of experts at α=0.05 significance level, using various statistical analyses (Table 2). Calculation of Content Validity Index (CVI)
The Content Validity Ratio (CVR) is a statistical tool used for the acceptance or rejection of specific items. Once items are defined to be included in the scale through the determination of CVR, the CVI is then calculated for the entire test. In this case, the mean of the CVR values of the items deemed appropriate for inclusion on the scale is calculated to obtain the CVI value. It is important to note that the content validity index should not be confused with the correlation coefficient. The CVI represents the degree of overlap observed between the functional capacity of a defined job performance domain and the performance observed in the test under investigation. Functionally, the CVI is the average percentage of overlap between the test items and the job performance domain (Lawshe, 1975).

discourses.source_txt: Accordingly, when Table 3 is examined, it is observed that after removing two items (Items 1 and 2) from the scale, the CVR values of 6 of the remaining 64 items (Items 4, 16, 27, 28, 29, and 30) are lower than the critical CVR value (CVRcritical = 0.385). Therefore, these 6 items, which fall below this critical value, were also removed from the draft scale being developed. As a result, 58 items remained in the sample scale. The CVI value for the sample study was calculated after removing 8 items from the scale and was determined to be 0.691.

Bu nedenle, bu kritik değerden aşağı düşen bu 6 öğe de geliştirilen ölçeğin taslak taslakından çıkarıldı. Sonuç olarak, 58 öğe örnek ölçeğinde kaldı.

discourses.source_txt: The fact that the obtained CVI value is greater than the CVRcritical value (CVI>CVRcritical) indicates that the content validity of the remaining items on the scale is statistically significant (Ateş Çobanoğlu, 2013; Batdı, 2013; Lawshe, 1975; Öngöz, 2011).
discourses.translated_txt: Alınan CVI değerin CVR eleştirel değeri (CVI>CVR eleştirel) üzerinde olması, ölçekteki kalan öğelerin içeriği geçerliliğinin istatistiksel olarak önemli olduğunu göstermektedir (Ateş Çobanoğlu, 2013; Batdı, 2013; Lawshe, 1975; Öngöz, 2011).

discourses.source_txt: In other words, when the CVI and CVRcritical values are compared, if the CVI value is less than the CVRcritical value, it is stated that the remaining items in the scale do not possess content validity (Lawshe, 1975). Accordingly, since the values obtained in the sample study indicate that the CVI (0.691) > CVRcritical (0.385), the content validity of the remaining items in the scale (58 items) is statistically significant.
discourses.translated_txt: Başka bir deyişle, CVI ve CVR kritik değerlerini karşılaştırırken, CVI değerinin CVR kritik değerinden daha düşük olması durumunda, ölçekteki kalan öğelerin içeriği geçerli olmadığını belirtir (Lawshe, 1975).

discourses.source_txt: After the content validity analyses of the sample study, the remaining 58 items for which at least one expert indicated a “needs revision” opinion were reviewed again and revised in line with expert feedback, and ultimately, a scale possessing content validity was obtained.
discourses.translated_txt: Örnek çalışmasının içeriği doğruluğu analizlerinden sonra, en az bir uzmanın bir revizyona ihtiyaçları  görüşünü belirttiği kalan 58 madde tekrar gözden geçirilmiş ve uzmanların geri bildirimlerine uygun olarak gözden geçirilmiş ve sonuçta içeriğe sahip bir ölçek elde edilmiştir.

discourses.source_txt:
Discussion and Conclusion
In this sample study, the content validity ratio and content validity index were introduced, and a roadmap was provided for conducting content analysis in scale development studies in a simple and practical way. In scale development studies, the reliability of the measurement tool is related to its stability. In this case, validity studies that consider what is intended to be measured with the measurement tool and whether the items measure accurately for their intended purpose come to the forefront.
discourses.translated_txt: Tartışma ve Sonuç Bu örnek çalışmasında, içerik geçerliliği oranı ve içerik geçerliliği indeksi tanıtıldı ve ölçek geliştirme çalışmalarında basit ve pratik bir şekilde içerik analizi gerçekleştirmek için bir yol haritası sağlandı. Ölçek geliştirme çalışmalarında, ölçüm araçının güvenilirliği sabitliği ile ilgilidir. Bu durumda, ölçüm aracı ile ölçülmeyi amaçlayan şeyleri ve öğelerin amaçlı amaçları için doğru ölçülüp ölçülmediğini inceleyen geçerlilik çalışmaları ön plana çıkar.

discourses.source_txt: The validity of measurement obtained from assessment tools will vary depending on the intended purpose of the measurement (Ercan & Kan, 2004; Kalaycı, 2016; Leech, Barrett, & Morgan, 2005). Content validity studies, which reveal the extent to which the scale and each item on the scale serve their intended purpose, are processes that convert qualitative studies based on expert opinions into statistical quantitative studies (Ercan & Kan, 2004; Shuttleworth, 2016; Yurdugül, 2005). Through this process, referred to as content analysis in scale development studies, the quality of the scale and its items is enhanced and procedural and temporal efficiency is achieved (Büyüköztürk, 2005; Demiralp & Kazu, 2012; Yurdugül, 2005). The qualifications of the experts are also highly important for ensuring consistent and unbiased results (Shuttleworth, 2016; Yurdugül, 2005). Consequently, by following the roadmap presented in this study, a useful scale with adequate content validity can be developed—one that offers advantages such as increasing construct validity for the targeted construct, conducting preliminary item analyses, and controlling the number of item factors.
discourses.translated_txt: Ölçüm araçlarından elde edilen ölçümlerin geçerliliği ölçümlerin amaçlı amacına bağlı olarak değişecektir (Ercan & Kan, 2004; Kalaycı, 2016; Leech, Barrett, & Morgan, 2005). Ölçü ve ölçekteki her öğenin amaçlı amaca ne kadar hizmet ettiğini ortaya koyan içerik geçerliliği çalışmaları, uzman görüşlerine dayanan niteliksel çalışmaları istatistiksel miktarlı çalışmalara dönüştüren süreçlerdir (Ercan & Kan, 2004; Shuttleworth, 2016; Yurdugül, 2005).
